title: Every Change Can Be Taken Back
summary: Almost anything you change in Abject can now be undone and redone with Ctrl+Z, from moving a dock item to deleting an object or a file. Deleting things no longer asks you to confirm first: it happens right away and shows a short notice you can undo from.
highlights: Undo and redo work everywhere: Ctrl+Z undoes; Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y redoes. The window you are in sends the request to whatever owns the data, and a short notice tells you what was undone.
The desktop app's Edit menu now has working Undo and Redo items.

Deleted objects and folders go to a trash that lasts for the current session plus three days (up to 200 items or 64 MB), so they can come back. The old confirmation dialogs are replaced by an undo notice.
Files overwritten or deleted through the file system can be restored, and removed skills go to a trash of their own.

Undo covers the dock and taskbar, themes, the scheduler, workspace details, app and object browsers, agents and triggers, the pinboard, the object editor, chats and conversations, the knowledge browser, settings, and the AI section of global settings (keys and secrets are never kept in undo history).
Each person and object gets its own undo history, so your Ctrl+Z only undoes your own changes, never someone else's in a shared space. Some histories are saved to disk so they survive a restart.
Text fields keep their own typing undo. When a field has nothing left to undo, Ctrl+Z goes to the window around it.
Script packages can mark a saveData call as undoable and get notified when their data is restored, so undo works in your own abjects too.

title: A dock you can search and keep favorites in
summary: The dock's Abjects section now has a search field and a favorites list, and its rows scroll inside a fixed header. Finding and opening the objects you use most takes fewer clicks.
highlights: Search the dock: a field at the top of the Abjects section filters the built-in apps and your own objects as you type, puts the best matches first, and opens the top match when you press Enter (Escape or the clear mark empties it)
Favorites: hover over an object's row and click the star to pin it to a favorites list above the rest; your favorites are saved between sessions
The dock's header and search field stay in place while only the rows below them scroll, so a long list of objects no longer pushes the controls out of view
The button that collapses or expands the dock has moved to a small icon at the right end of the System header, next to the gear, so the old toggle row at the top is gone
Scrollbars across the interface are hidden until you need them: a thin thumb shows while you hover or scroll, and it widens to a full bar when the pointer is over it
Labels too long for a dock row now fade out at the edge instead of ending in an ellipsis; hover to see the full name
Widgets that scripts and packages can use: buttons can carry a small action icon at their right end, text fields can have a leading icon and a clear mark, and there are new star and sidebar icons
fixes: Clicking a dock row no longer leaves a red focus box around it; the focus ring now appears only when you move focus with the keyboard
Hidden rows in a scrolling list no longer take up scroll height, so lists no longer end in empty space

title: Windows Close Cleanly, Quiet Models Recover
summary: This small stability release fixes windows that could be torn down twice when closed. It also stops agents from failing when an OpenAI-compatible model returns no text.
highlights: Closing a window now tears it down exactly once: a second close request waits for the first instead of repeating it, and other objects hear only one "window destroyed" notice

When an OpenAI-compatible model (including OpenRouter) returns no text, for example because it spent its whole budget on reasoning or refused, the request is retried right away; if the retries also come back empty, the caller gets an empty answer it already knows how to handle instead of failing
fixes: Fixed a crash ("Cannot read properties of null") in LLM calls when a provider returned a completion with no text content; retries and provider fallbacks now treat it as an empty completion
Fixed windows that kept sending drawing updates after closing began, which produced "no surface" errors from the display server
A handler that stops only because its object was shut down is now logged as normal teardown, not as an error, which removes the "Object stopped" noise when widgets close in the middle of a render
Empty-completion errors now include the finish reason, token usage and any refusal text, so it is easier to see why a model returned nothing

title: Room to Read the Whole Thing
summary: Agents now size what they read and keep to the context window of the model they actually run on. Models with large windows stop clipping and paging work they have room for, and objects that save often stop rewriting storage that has not changed.
highlights: Every provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Gemini, DeepSeek, Grok, Kimi, Meta, PeerLLM and the CLI agents) now reports each model's real context window. A hosted model whose provider gives no window is looked up in the public OpenRouter catalog. Before this, every OpenRouter model got a small fixed budget, even ones with a million-token window.

Agents scale what one step shows them (job results, observations, file pages, grep output, review transcripts) to the model they last thought on. Each has a floor, so small or unknown windows behave as before; large windows stop truncating and paging.
ObjectCreator shows a large object's source whole when the model has room for it, instead of paging through a few thousand lines at a time.
Attached text files in Chat, preloaded skill instructions and goal-review transcripts are sized to the tier that reads them, not to one fixed number.

A script abject can now answer ask and describe itself, and still reach the system's version through super.ask(msg) and super.describe(msg). The system keeps answering ask while the object is busy, and describe always carries the real manifest.
ObjectCreator can verify an object that draws straight into the desktop scene without a window: it uses a desktop capture as the visual check instead of refusing the work.
fixes: Objects that save their state as they run no longer rewrite an unchanged source, manifest and index on every save. Only changed data is written, and nothing at all when the data is the same.
ObjectCreator now flags handler members whose names collide with a system handler, and explains that super works only in method syntax.

title: Work in progress stays in progress
summary: This is a small release about trust. Agents no longer deploy an edit that was made against an older copy of an object, and they now talk about your work in the words you use, showing you the finished result instead of every step on the way.
highlights: When an agent edits an object that changed after its draft was started (by you, by another task, or by an earlier deploy), it now sets the old draft aside with a note explaining why, instead of deploying it over the newer changes
When a task finishes, its chat now shows one screenshot of the final result; screenshots of half-finished work stay out of the conversation
Agents now name things the way you see them (a window by its title, a file by its name) and leave out ids, storage keys and technical counts unless you ask how something was done
Cards now state facts in plain terms (where, when, how much) and leave internal ids out
Agents can take a screenshot of a window by its window id, so they don't have to look up which object owns it first
fixes: Colors written without a leading '#' (for example 'a8683c') in generated drawing code and gradients now show the intended color; before, they painted black
One bad entry in the object registry can no longer break every lookup in a workspace until restart; the bad entry is dropped and logged
Object storage and the registry now reject a missing object id, where before it could slip through and corrupt the registry
When an agent sends an edit with nothing in it, it is now told which fields it did send, so it stops repeating the same empty edit

title: Sleeping Objects You Can Keep
summary: You can now keep the objects you care about: they sleep in folders until something needs them, and they show on your own board as live cards. The built-in browser also gets through bot checks such as Cloudflare Turnstile again.
highlights: Kept objects: you can keep named objects in folders, where they sleep while nobody is using them. When another object or agent asks for one, it wakes up, so nothing has to stay running just to stay available.

A board of your own: the new pinboard shows your kept objects as cards, and any object that can draw itself appears inline in a slot. A slot keeps its last picture as a preview, uses your theme's colours and fonts, and passes your clicks and typing to the object.
Shorter goal rows in Chat: each goal now reads as one sentence, and goal cards have a plain headline you can take in at a glance.
Tap to answer: when Chat, a running goal or a dialog asks you a question, it offers short answers you can tap instead of typing.
fixes: The built-in browser now passes bot checks such as Cloudflare Turnstile. Before, it told pages it was plain Chrome, but those checks look at what the browser can do rather than what it says, so they failed every time, even when a person clicked the challenge.

title: Goals you can watch, calls you can stop
summary: Running goals now show up as live cards that tell you what each agent is doing as it does it, and stopping an AI call ends it right away. Notes you add partway through a goal reach the right agent, and the plan only changes when your note calls for it.
highlights: Goal cards: each goal shows its state, question, plan, tasks, result and notes on one card, and every running task keeps a short trail of its recent steps. In chat, a running goal appears as a live card with timers that tick every second.
The Goals window now has the list beside the open card, with filters and search; on narrow screens (below 760 px) it shows one pane at a time.
Task progress is easier to read: a task shows "step 3" and only names its step limit near the end ("step 27 of 30 · 3 left"), because the limit is a ceiling, not an estimate of the work.
Goal cards say what an agent is actually doing (for example "call SettingsManager.ask: How do I create a preset") rather than only the verb it used.

Kill in the LLM monitor now stops a call immediately, even before its first word arrives; a stopped call is not retried or sent to another provider. The OpenAI provider closes its connection, and abject-backed providers receive a new providerCancel message (documented in docs/LLM_PROVIDERS.md and the script SDK types).

Notes added during a goal are checked against the tasks in progress and the agents doing them: a note that changes the work, or makes it another agent's kind of work, replans right away, while one that fits the current plan waits for the next planning step.

Changes to settings, presets, records and other data an existing object keeps are handled by messaging that object. Writing a new object, or changing what an existing one does, is left to the object-creation agent.
fixes: On Wayland, web pages running offscreen can no longer open native dialogs (confirm, print, file picker), which could crash the desktop app.
A cancelled question now counts as declined; a question nobody answered is still treated as unanswered.
Actions where the model nests its arguments under the action's name are now read correctly instead of failing.
A registered external project can only be replaced by name by a trust authority, not by any caller.
When a class has several instances (Name, Name-2, ...), caller identity now carries the shared manifest name, so they are recognized as the same kind of object.

title: Your Notes Reach the Agents Doing the Work
summary: When you add a note to a running goal, the agents already working on it now get that note at their next step, not just at the next planning round. Agents also start each task with a briefing on where the goal stands, including any notes you have left.
highlights: Notes you add while a goal is running now go straight to every agent working on that goal or its sub-goals; each agent sees your note at its next step, so a change of plan takes effect mid-task.
Each agent's task briefing now lists the notes left on its goal and on the goals above it, so an agent that starts later still knows what you asked for.
fixes: Agents no longer stumble when they judge a step from a record that is only partly written.
Patterns an agent applied are now recorded as ids, so the agent learns from the right pattern after a task.
The task reviewer copes better with unusual cases when it looks back over finished work.

title: Leaking abjects restart; the rest keep running
summary: When an abject's code uses too much memory, Abject now works out which abject is responsible and restarts only that one, with its data intact, so the rest of its worker thread keeps running instead of running out of memory. The agy provider also works again on agy 1.3.4, with its newer models available.
highlights: Per-abject memory accounting: memory use is now measured inside each sandboxed abject, so heap usage is pinned on the abject whose code holds it instead of being guessed.

Automatic relief for leaking abjects: a user abject holding more than a quarter of its thread's memory ceiling (or the largest one when a thread or the shared heap is near its limit) is restarted in a fresh sandbox with its data kept. If it fills up again within ten minutes, it is stopped instead, and its saved copy is kept.
Built-in objects are never restarted for memory; only user-created and package abjects are. This works in the desktop, headless and p2p editions.
agy provider model list refreshed for agy 1.3.4: Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are now selectable (thanks to andreBurnt).

The README has been rewritten as a project landing page: screenshots up front, the Ask Protocol as the central idea, and one Configuration section with environment variables and the Ollama walkthrough.
fixes: Requests routed through the agy provider failed on agy 1.3.4 because the tier defaults still named retired Gemini 3.7 Flash models. The defaults now use Gemini 3.8 Flash at the same effort levels.
Saved settings that point at retired agy models (older Flash and Pro lines, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 Thinking) are moved to their current successors when settings load.
These model migrations now also apply to the vision, fallback and decision model choices, not just the tier choices, so a fallback pinned to a retired model no longer keeps failing.

title: Patterns From Lessons That Keep Coming Back
summary: Your workspace now turns lessons it keeps relearning into written patterns. Until now a lesson only became a pattern if it had been flagged as a candidate the first time it showed up, so a new workspace could run dozens of goals and still have no patterns at all.
highlights: The task reviewer now notices when the same piece of knowledge has come up in more than one goal, and offers those cases to the pattern language as instances of one recurring problem to name and write down as a pattern.
The context the reviewer reads before each goal now lists knowledge met in two or more goals, next to the existing patterns and candidate lessons, so a fresh workspace has something to build on.
KnowledgeBase 3.9.0 counts how many separate goals relied on each entry, and recall can now be limited to entries seen in at least a given number of goals (the new minGoals option).
fixes: When the reviewer judged an ordinary lesson as if it were a pattern, the update used to fail with "Pattern not found" and be discarded. It now counts as confirming, disputing or leaving that lesson unchanged, so the judgment is kept.

title: Shell permission prompts in plain words
summary: When an abject asks to run a shell command, the permission prompt now opens with a short, everyday explanation of what the command will do, so you can decide with confidence even if you don't read shell. The exact command and its analysis stay on screen right below that explanation.
highlights: Shell permission prompts start with a plain-language summary of what the command does, written by your fast-tier model from the command analysis; the exact command stays visible beneath it, and the model only explains (you still make the decision)
The explanation shows up wherever you answer: the desktop permission window, and the question lists in the `abject` command and its chat TUI

The model sees only the redacted command, its answers are cached so repeated prompts open quickly, and it has a 20-second limit; with no model configured, or if it fails or takes too long, the prompt opens just as it did before

title: A Sealed Sandbox for Script Abjects
summary: Generated objects, script packages, agent jobs and trigger rules now run in a rebuilt sandbox. Nothing of the host is reachable from inside it, and every stretch of code has a time limit, so a buggy or hostile script can no longer get past your permissions or freeze the system.
highlights: Script abjects (generated objects and script packages) run in a new sandbox with hard isolation: nothing from the host process is in reach, and messages, replies and this.data cross the boundary only as copies (JSON values and Uint8Array).

Every stretch of sandboxed code has a time limit. A handler or timer callback may run 1 s without pausing; past that, the call fails and the object keeps its state and keeps running instead of locking up its worker.
Each agent job gets its own sandbox, now with setTimeout and setInterval. A job's code may run 10 s without pausing, and the error says how to split longer work into pieces.

Jobs can take an optional timeoutMs that stops them after a stretch with no progress (at most a day). Each answered call and each progress report starts that clock over, including progress from an object the job is waiting on.
Long work can wait longer: a job's call to another object now waits up to a day for its answer instead of 10 minutes.
A job waiting on something that can never arrive (no call outstanding, no timer set) now fails at once with a reason instead of hanging.
Errors in script and job code now report line numbers, and pnpm forge runs the same checks as the runtime, so a package that installs will load. import() is refused up front.
Editing a script abject's source swaps it in place and keeps its this.data.
Trigger rule filters and payload templates are checked when the rule is saved, compiled once per rule, and limited to 250 ms per evaluation.
Running from source now needs Node.js 22.8 or newer; abject doctor checks for it.
fixes: Closed a hole where sandboxed code could reach the host process through objects handed into the sandbox, and from there get past PermissionBroker.
Agent jobs had no time limit, so a runaway loop in job code could tie up a worker for good; it is now stopped.
A scheduled job that ran longer than a minute was fired again on every scheduler tick while the first run was still going; a schedule now waits for its running job to finish.
Timers set by a script abject or a job now stop when the object stops, its source is replaced, or the job ends, instead of running on.

title: Remote MCP servers, with sign-in
summary: Abject can now connect to MCP servers hosted on the web, not only ones it launches on your own machine, and handles the sign-in those servers ask for. Images that tools return now show up in chat as pictures.
highlights: Connect to a remote MCP server by its URL: Abject speaks the Streamable HTTP transport and falls back to the older HTTP+SSE transport when a server needs it, and a session restarts cleanly if the server forgets it

OAuth sign-in for servers that require it: Abject finds the server's sign-in details, opens the approval page in your browser and listens for the reply on your machine (or lets you paste the code). It caches the token and refreshes it; only the connection that asked for a token can read it
Skills can describe remote servers with new fields (mcp-url, mcp-headers, mcp-oauth-client-id); header values like ${API_KEY} are read from your environment, so secrets stay out of SKILL.md
The catalog can now install hosted MCP servers. If a server needs you to approve access, the catalog shows 'Sign in to finish' and the skill list shows that it is waiting for you to sign in
Host MCP import now finds remote servers you have already set up in other tools, along with local ones
Images returned by MCP tools now appear in chat: they are saved to the workspace's files and shown inline
fixes: MCP tool results that contained images lost them and showed only a '[image: image/png]' placeholder (this is why requests like 'show the QR code' failed)
Long dialog messages, such as a sign-in address, were cut off and could not be selected; dialogs now size themselves to the message, scroll when it is very long, and let you select and copy the text

title: Fewer Ghost Messages, Windows You Can Close
summary: A small maintenance release: objects that have stopped no longer keep receiving events, and the planning agents now follow your requests about how results should appear more faithfully, including keeping a close button on new windows.
highlights: When you ask for something like a diagram, Chat passes along only the constraints you actually stated; it no longer adds its own choices about how or where the result appears, so it stops turning a plain request into a borderless desktop object you can't close

Planning agents read your follow-up notes the way you see your screen: if you say "put it in a window", you get a real window with a title bar you can move and close, and the team re-plans when a delivered result doesn't look the way you asked
Fewer wasted messages in long sessions: closed chats and stopped objects stop receiving updates, which keeps logs quieter and frees up work for the rest of the system
fixes: Objects that stopped without unsubscribing (for example, a closed chat still getting goal updates) are now dropped from their subscriptions the first time a message to them can't be delivered, which ends the flood of undeliverable-message warnings
The window manager forgets widgets that were stopped without being explicitly removed (layout children, released widgets), so theme changes are no longer broadcast to widgets that no longer exist

title: The desktop trusts a healthy GPU again
summary: This is a small fix to v0.15.5. On some machines with a working graphics card, the desktop app switched to software rendering when it didn't need to. Now it only does that when WebGL is really turned off or unavailable.
highlights: The safety net from v0.15.5 still works: if the graphics card gives the desktop no WebGL (blocklisted, acceleration turned off, or a driver mismatch), the app falls back to software rendering instead of sitting on the splash screen.
fixes: Fixed the desktop app switching to software rendering on a healthy graphics card. It used to check WebGL right at startup, before the graphics process had reported in, and at that moment Chromium says every feature is off. It now waits for the graphics card's real status and falls back only when WebGL actually turns off; WebGL already running in software no longer counts as off.

title: Sharp windows on high-resolution screens
summary: Text and graphics inside windows now render crisply on HiDPI and Retina displays instead of looking soft, and stay sharp when you zoom, switch displays or open Exposé. A small fix also lets the backend shut down cleanly.
highlights: Windows now draw at your screen's pixel density (up to 2x), so text and widgets are crisp on HiDPI and Retina displays; nothing changes on a standard 1x screen

Windows redraw at the right resolution when the pixel ratio changes (browser zoom, moving to another display, or entering and leaving mobile mode), so they stay sharp rather than showing scaled-up old pixels
Text no longer shimmers in windows shown smaller than full size (Exposé, windows pushed back or tilted in the 3D desktop)
Phones keep window surfaces at 1x so memory stays in check, since a phone holds every window while showing one at a time
fixes: Fixed soft, blurry text in windows on HiDPI screens; click targets and shadows are scaled to match the sharper surfaces
Fixed the HTTP exchange recorder (CassetteRecorder) retrying a flush forever after it was stopped, which could keep the process from exiting on shutdown

title: Asks Before Acting, Learns Within Budget
summary: Abject now asks you before a click, form submission or tool call that would change something, and you can set a daily dollar limit on what it spends learning. Learned knowledge takes far less space, chat messages show when they were sent, goal progress shows only real work, and the remote link reconnects on its own.
highlights: Asks before consequential actions: the web browser works out what a click, key press or form submit would do and asks your permission first; an MCP tool its server marks as destructive runs only after you approve it.

Daily learning budget: Settings → AI has a daily learning budget in US dollars. Abject tracks what each part of the system spends on models each day, and reviews hold off as the day's budget runs low. Settings also gain a number field type, editable in the window and from the `abject` command.

Leaner learning: evidence such as task records and observations is stored once and cited by reference, so a single belief no longer carries copies of other goals' transcripts. KnowledgeBase 3.8.0 compacts older learning history and no longer rewrites an entry each time it is recalled.
The Knowledge browser has a new Learning tab that shows how observations become knowledge.
Chat messages show when they were sent: "now" for the first minute, the clock time for today and the date and time for earlier days. Replayed history groups by send time.

Goal progress shows real work: a collaborator's goal shows its latest progress line, phase and agent instead of a generic placeholder. Watchdog heartbeats and repeated reasoning no longer fill the progress feed.
The remote link heals itself: it checks its signaling connection every minute and rebuilds a client that has been down for longer than its retries cover.
The desktop app falls back when the graphics card fails to start, and the client shows a notice when it cannot reach its backend.
fixes: Test failure counts now come from the test runner's full output, not a truncated preview that mixed test names with error lines.
Knowledge updates repeated in a review's correction round are no longer written twice, and a repair or curation pass no longer overwrites the verdict a goal review shows you.

Learning waits until a workspace has finished starting before calling a model, keeps settling decisions after the first repair starts and drops repairs aimed at knowledge entries that no longer exist.
When a model sends its reading of a prediction as a separate action, that reading now rides on the next action instead of disrupting batching.
OpenRouter attribution headers now default to abject.world and "Abject" instead of placeholder values.

title: The whole desktop, on a machine with no screen
summary: Abject now ships a server edition: the full desktop backend packaged to run on a headless Linux machine, which you open from any browser by pairing. Nothing listens publicly; the browser and the server meet through the peer network.
highlights: New server edition: Linux release archives (abject-server-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz) carry the complete desktop backend, so a machine with no screen can run the same desktop you would use locally.

Open the server's desktop from a browser with a one-use pairing link, made in Settings (Auth) or by an abject that asks RemoteUIAccess for one; the UI WebSocket stays on loopback, and the browser reaches the server through signaling.

The server archive installs and runs the same way as the headless edition (same layout, same abject.service, same `abject serve`); two settings in abject.env point it at your browser client and signaling server.
The `abject` command recognizes a server install: serve, stop, restart, status and doctor all work with it, and `abject doctor` reports it as the server edition.
`abject update` keeps each install on its own edition: a server install updates from the server archive and a headless install from the headless one.
The deployment guide has a new section, The desktop on a server, that covers setup, the two environment variables and how pairing works.
Building from source: `pnpm incarnate:server` packages the server edition.

title: A Headless Edition and the abject Command
summary: Abject now runs without a desktop, on a server, in a container or as a background service, and you can manage and talk to it from the new `abject` command in your terminal. Under the hood, an object's trust now depends on how it was built, which closes a way for user code to pass itself off as part of the system.
highlights: New headless edition: the same backend runs with no display, so you can run Abject on a server, in Docker, or as a system service. A build check confirms that no display code gets into the headless bundle.
The `abject` command is now a full CLI. It has a chat interface in the terminal plus setup, doctor, locate, connect, service and update subcommands, and the desktop app includes it.
New ways to install: a Dockerfile, Homebrew, Scoop and Winget manifests, one-line install scripts for Linux, macOS and Windows on abject.world, and a single-binary package of the headless edition.
Questions from your objects (confirmations and prompts) now reach you wherever you are: in a window on the desktop, or in the terminal through the `abject` command.

Each running backend writes a small instance file (process, edition, ports, owner token) to its data directory. The `abject` command uses it to find and connect to the backend, and AuthGate checks every connection.

Trust now comes from how an object was built. Only objects compiled into the server are treated as built in. Scripts, WASM packages, proxies and remote objects can no longer claim system privileges by copying a name or ID pattern.
Spawning, killing, cloning and registering objects, plus writes to saved object data, now follow that rule, so user code works only with its own objects and its own registry entries.

The old manifest capability system is gone; PermissionBroker remains what decides access to files, the shell and the network. Manifests saved before this release still load, because outdated capability entries are now ignored.
Negotiated proxies between objects now hold wherever the two objects run (main thread, the same worker or different workers), and self-healing still keeps track of how well each proxy is working.
Every directory in the source tree has a README, and the architecture, CLAUDE.md and philosophy docs have been rewritten to match the current code.
fixes: Closed a hole where a user-written object could take a system object's name or typeId pattern and gain privileged access to the Factory, Registry, Supervisor or saved object data.
The app updater, browser window host and external project registry used guesswork based on names and IDs to decide whom to trust; they now use the same built-in check as everything else.
Per-workspace objects are now registered on both the main thread and the worker threads, so they no longer fail to start in a worker without any error.

title: Your Own Workspace Can Change Its Settings
summary: Abjects and agents in a workspace you host locally can now change global settings for you, so asking an agent to switch models or adjust a permission no longer sends you to the Settings window. Shared, public, and joined workspaces still can't change settings, and only the Settings window can read saved credentials back.
highlights: Abjects and agents in a local workspace hosted on your own machine can now change global settings: AI tiers and keys, presets, permissions, and the other sections the Settings window covers. Before this, only the Settings window and the commune terminal client could make these changes.
Agents in a local workspace can apply, save, and delete model presets and record command rules and skill grants; this lets a request like "switch to the cheaper preset" finish in one step.

Shared and public workspaces still can't write settings, and neither can a local copy of a workspace you joined from another peer. If the system can't confirm that the caller's workspace is one you host locally, it refuses the change.
Reading secrets back (API keys and other credentials) is still limited to the Settings window; no workspace abject can read them.

title: Native Knowledge and a Living Pattern Language
summary: Your workspace's knowledge now lives in a native WebAssembly KnowledgeBase, and goal reviews now read the pattern language stored there. Lessons that keep coming back turn into full patterns on their own, so the system learns from the kinds of work you actually do.
highlights: The KnowledgeBase is now a native C++ WebAssembly package that ships with the app and loads at every boot. The old TypeScript version is gone. It is marked as required, so the app stops at startup if the KnowledgeBase is missing instead of running without its memory.

Goal reviews now see your workspace's pattern language next to the record of what happened: the patterns that matched the work, patterns that are referenced but not yet written, and candidate lessons shown beside the matching patterns. Each section has a size limit so the goal itself always has room.

Recurring lessons become patterns automatically: when a review sees work that repeats an earlier candidate lesson, the reviewer promotes that lesson to a full pattern instead of waiting for someone to do it by hand.
Plans can say which patterns they intend to use, and those choices are now recorded in the KnowledgeBase. Reviews show which of those patterns have recorded applications and which do not.
Pattern weaving can now start from patterns already in use and follow their links, can be limited by scope, and records a 'no effect' verdict alongside helpful, harmful and inconclusive.

WebAssembly packages can include an ask guide: a usage guide in markdown, plus the model tier for answers, that is added to the abject's ask prompt so others can learn how to work with it. `pnpm forge` installs the guide with the module. Packages can also be marked required.

title: Stalled Goals Wake Up Again
summary: Goals that used to sit idle with no work left in flight now get noticed and reviewed, so they either start moving again or fail cleanly instead of hanging. Agents also handle more models correctly, including those that write tool calls in their own native format.
highlights: Stalled goals get a second look: when an active goal has nothing running, queued or left to do, the team holds a review scrum to restart it, and if two reviews in a row leave it stuck, the goal is marked failed so it stops hanging
Agents now read a model's native tool-call markup as actions instead of plain text, so models that use their own tool-call format work properly
Work that a goal's task starts now belongs to that same goal, and goal health checks count queued work, so progress reporting is more accurate
fixes: Cancelling a goal's outstanding tasks no longer cancels the task that asked for the cleanup, which had been stopping goals partway through
A planning round whose scrum was cancelled with nothing to replace it now runs again instead of leaving the goal waiting
Retries waiting on backoff count as a scrum still to come, so they are no longer mistaken for a stall

title: Settings from the terminal, instances in your pocket
summary: You can now read and change every global setting from the commune terminal client, and one browser or phone can hold several Abject instances and switch between them. Window screenshots also work for windows that are hidden, covered, or in another workspace.
highlights: Edit settings from the terminal: commune gains /settings, /get, /set, /add, /wset, /preset apply, /skill enable and /update check, in both the tabbed TUI and the plain REPL; keys and passwords are hidden as you type and never shown again

The p2p client can remember several instances and show one at a time: a pill on desktop (Ctrl+Shift+O) or a sheet on your phone lists them, your choice is saved, and the picker, connecting screen and login card all say which instance you are on

Global settings now live in a dedicated SettingsManager that saves them, checks every change, applies it to AI, UI and permissions right away, and announces the change; the Settings window is now just its view
Updates can be checked, downloaded and installed from the terminal as well as from the Settings window
Window screenshots work wherever the window is: off-screen, under other windows, or in another workspace, and everything is put back afterwards
fixes: Changing capability enforcement in Settings now takes effect immediately
Objects can no longer move a window into a different workspace; only the workspace system can, and other objects can only place a new object in their own workspace

title: Updates that install while the app runs
summary: This release changes when the desktop app installs updates. Installation now begins while Abject is still running normally instead of at the very end of shutdown, so a crash or a slow exit can no longer leave an update half-installed or skipped.
highlights: Updates now start installing while the app is running and healthy. After a restart, the new version is launched by a small separate helper once the old process has fully exited.
Linux AppImage: once a download is verified, the new AppImage replaces the old one right away. The new version runs the next time you launch or restart.
Windows: the installer starts when you choose Restart to Update, or as soon as the app begins to quit, and then finishes after the app has closed.

Linux .deb: the package installs during Restart to Update, so the password prompt shows up while the app is still open. You get up to five minutes to answer it, and if you close the prompt the app keeps running and tries again on the next attempt.
The status messages in Settings → Updates, the workspace update notification and the README now describe what happens for each type of install.
fixes: Fixed updates that could be lost when a native crash or the exit watchdog ended shutdown before the installer had finished.

title: The app now updates itself
summary: Abject's desktop app can now find, download and install new versions without you visiting the website. Install v0.14.6 by hand once; releases after it arrive on their own.
highlights: The packaged desktop app checks GitHub releases for new versions, downloads them in the background and installs them when you quit, or right away when you choose Restart to Update.

How updates install depends on how you installed the app: the Windows installer and AppImage update in place; .deb installs update only when you restart, because dpkg asks for your password; macOS builds are unsigned for now, so they offer the new DMG as a manual download.

A new Updates tab in Settings shows update status and download progress, with buttons to check now, download, restart, and read the release notes. It also lets you turn automatic downloading on or off.
A workspace notification tells you when a new version is downloaded and ready to install.
The Help menu has a new Check for Updates... item, which opens Settings on the Updates tab.
Only the Settings window can download an update, restart the app or change the auto-download setting. Other objects can check for updates and read the status, but they cannot start an install.
The headless server package does not include the updater; server deployments keep updating the way they do now.

title: Headless servers, web pages, and a locked door
summary: Abject can now run as a headless server, and script packages can serve web pages, join workspace profiles, and use a new Crypto capability. This release also closes a hole that let any web page open on your machine connect to Abject's UI socket.
highlights: Script packages can serve web pages: in http mode a package answers WebRequest messages with WebResponses, and its cookies are scoped to its own route (see docs/WEB_GATEWAY.md).
Headless server packaging: pnpm incarnate:server builds a self-contained server bundle with a systemd unit, and a new InstanceInfo abject reports the running version and answers GET /healthz.

Workspace profiles decide which abjects a workspace spawns. There are built-in default and service profiles, you can override them with a profiles.json, and packages declare which profiles they join (see docs/WORKSPACE_PROFILES.md).

The UI WebSocket now accepts connections only from the desktop app, the dev client, and origins you list in ABJECTS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS (for reverse-proxied clients). Before this, any web page open in a browser on the same machine could connect and drive the UI.
New Crypto capability for script packages: random bytes and UUIDs, hashes and HMACs, password hashing and verification, timing-safe comparison, byte encoding, and signature verification.
System-scope script packages run once per instance instead of once per workspace, and the Packages abject keeps their data.
Packages tagged launcher that have show and hide methods get a row in the dock's System section, with the name and icon from their manifest; clicking the row opens them.
The desktop app moves from Electron 35 to Electron 44, so the app and its built-in web browser run on a current Chromium.
fixes: Pairing QR codes and images embedded in markdown decode correctly again; a shared encoding module replaces the old ad hoc base64 handling.
Peers keep accurate routes to each other: route announcements are versioned and sent as diffs, and a full reconnect now triggers a complete resync.
A peer added to a shared workspace's whitelist after sharing now shows up in discovery, instead of being filtered out by a stale cached list.
Deleting a shared workspace now unshares it, so a new workspace with the same name can be found by the peers it is shared with.
A workspace created while the server is running is now served under its name on the web gateway, not under its internal id.

title: Your Own Models, Your Own Peers
summary: You can now add any model endpoint to Abjects as a package, without changing the server. You can also decide exactly which peers and signaling servers your instance talks to. Outgoing web requests no longer reach your local network unless you allow it.
highlights: Abjects can now be LLM providers: any abject (usually an autostart script package) can register with the LLM object and answer model calls by message. It appears in Settings → AI and gets tier routing, fallbacks, goal budgets, streaming and the cost ledger, the same as a built-in provider. The protocol is described in docs/LLM_PROVIDERS.md.

New example package, openai-compatible-provider: point it at any endpoint that speaks the OpenAI API (a local model server or a gateway) by setting a base URL, an optional API key and a list of models. The script SDK now includes types for writing your own providers.

Who Can Connect: a new card in the Network window that lets only the peers you list connect. Admission is checked on every incoming offer and before every outgoing connection, then again on the peer's verified identity once the encrypted handshake finishes. Removing a peer disconnects it. Servers can start this way with ABJECTS_PEER_ADMISSION=allowlist and ABJECTS_ALLOWED_PEERS.

Fixed signaling: the new "Use only these servers" checkbox under Network → Servers & Peers (or ABJECTS_SIGNALING_URLS) keeps an instance on your own signaling servers. It skips the public default and ignores servers learned from peers and contacts, so a private Whisper server stays private.

Private-address protection for web requests: HttpClient and StreamClient now refuse localhost, your local network, link-local and cloud metadata addresses. The check runs on what the host resolves to and again on every redirect. To allow a local service, add it under Settings → Permissions → Private hosts as a name, an address or a range (for example localhost:11434 for a local model server).
fixes: Quitting the app no longer leaves MCP servers, coding CLI sessions or other child processes running. They are signalled first thing at shutdown, and anything that ignores the request is force-stopped. This also fixes the AppImage build failing to finish quitting because a leftover server still held its mount.
Shutdown now finishes within the desktop app's quit deadline: the worker pool stops alongside the rest of teardown, and each worker-hosted object gets at most 2.5 seconds.

Connected peers are limited to the route announcement protocol. A peer can no longer register or remove routes directly, report false hop counts, or claim an object that is already reachable through another peer.
HTTP redirects to a different origin no longer carry your credential headers.

title: Bring your own abjects, in TypeScript
summary: You can now add abjects to an Abject instance by writing a small TypeScript or JavaScript package; you no longer need to change the server or compile to WebAssembly. Packages are turned on, turned off and configured from a new Packages tab in Settings, so one release can be set up as a different kind of instance for each person or team.
highlights: Script packages: write an abject as a plain JavaScript handler map (or in TypeScript, with full type definitions in sdk/script) and it runs in the same sandbox as abjects made in the app, on the worker pool

pnpm forge now builds script packages: it compiles TypeScript, checks that the result runs as a handler map in the sandbox, validates the manifest and settings, warns about declared methods with no handler, and installs the package; a plain .js package with a manifest needs no build step at all
New Packages tab in Settings: see every installed package, enable or disable each one, add package directories, and fill in the settings a package asks for (including secrets such as API tokens)
Packages can declare their own settings in abject.json; the Packages tab shows them as a form, and the package's abjects read them back by message

Packages load from several places in a predictable order: bundled native packages, installed extensions, the ABJECTS_PACKAGE_DIRS environment variable, and directories added in Settings; a newer version wins and an older copy never downgrades a type
A package can replace a built-in object type by name, so you can swap in your own version of a system service without forking the code
Package abjects are owned by their package and stay read-only in the editor; their saved data is kept in its own area so it doesn't mix with your other abjects

packages.json can be written by provisioning tools before first boot to set up an instance ahead of time; a malformed file is ignored and the defaults apply, so a typo won't stop the instance from starting
Two working examples to start from: tally-ts (TypeScript, with settings) and scene-showcase (plain JavaScript, no build), plus a new guide in docs/PACKAGES.md

title: The browser agent gets hands and eyes
summary: The web agent can now use a page the way a person does: it looks at a screenshot, then clicks, drags, scrolls and types with real mouse and keyboard input. Sites built from canvases, sliders and custom widgets, which the page outline can't name, are now within reach.
highlights: The web agent can click, hover, drag, scroll and type at any point on the visible page using real mouse and keyboard events, so it can work with canvases, sliders, hover menus, drag-and-drop and slide-to-verify controls
A new look action lets the agent take a screenshot in the same pixel coordinates it clicks in, so what it sees and where it points match exactly
Every pointer action reports which element it landed on, so the agent can check that it hit the right control before going further

The agent's guidance now helps it choose between two ways of acting: by reference to a named element (precise, and safe when the layout shifts) or by pointing at what the screenshot shows (for controls nothing else can name); retry and confirmation rules are also tighter

The same pointer and keyboard operations (clickAt, hoverAt, drag, scroll, typeText) are available on the web-browser capability for any Abject to use, and screenshotPage has a new scale option to match their coordinates
fixes: Clicking a hidden, collapsed or zero-size element now fails right away with a clear message that suggests what to do next, instead of silently missing
Elements parked off the page (often hidden duplicates of a visible control) are now detected and reported, so the agent picks the visible one instead
When a long page outline gets cut off, the agent is told where the cut happened and that it can scroll or use the screenshot to see the rest

title: Steadier hands in the web browser
summary: This patch release makes agents more reliable when they work in web pages. Clicks and form entries on busy sites and single-page apps no longer get rejected as stale, and scripts run in a page now return the values they compute.
highlights: Agents act on web pages more reliably: a page snapshot now stays valid until a genuinely new page loads. Route changes inside single-page apps and iframe loads no longer make every element reference look out of date.

When an element an agent wants to click or type into has disappeared from the page, the action now fails right away with a clear message asking for a fresh snapshot. It no longer waits out a long timeout and then lands on whatever happens to be there.
fixes: Fixed agents having their browser actions rejected or retried over and over on busy sites, where nearly every element reference was treated as stale just after the snapshot was taken.

Fixed in-page scripts losing their result when they contained the word "return" (for example inside a callback or a self-invoking function). Scripts now run as written and are wrapped only when they truly need a top-level return or await.
Browser actions on elements that never become usable now give up after 15 seconds, while the caller is still waiting for the answer.

title: One Browser Inside, Steadier Chat Windows
summary: The desktop app's web browser now runs on the Chromium already built into the app, so there is no second browser to download and logins carry over more reliably. Chat windows also stop flickering and jumping around while you move or resize them.
highlights: In the desktop app, web browsing now uses the Chromium the app already ships with, instead of downloading and bundling a separate headless browser; outside the desktop app, browsing works the same as before
Smaller desktop install, since the separate browser download and its packaging are gone
Quitting the desktop app now saves cookies from every open browser window first, so a login you just completed is kept for next time
If you open the desktop app a second time, the second copy no longer points the browser at a debugging connection that has already closed
fixes: Dragging a chat window no longer moves that conversation to the top of the list or rebuilds the conversation overview several times a second; the window still reopens where you left it
The conversation list now updates in place, so it no longer blinks empty while histories load and keeps your search text and scroll position
Resizing a chat no longer makes the welcome card flash; it re-fits in place

title: Faster Boots and Self-Updating Model Tiers
summary: Abject now starts faster on long-lived workspaces and keeps each model tier pointed at your provider's newest models without manual upkeep. Agents also recover more gracefully when a plan step is rejected or a website puts up a human-verification wall.
highlights: Model tiers now follow each provider's latest models, so new releases are picked up without editing your settings.
Faster startup on large workspaces: shared state is restored in batches at boot, and sync is scoped to the workspace it belongs to.
Finished goals are moved to a cold archive, and goal updates no longer rewrite whole records, which keeps the active store small.
Mobile: a new Exposé button sits next to the quick command button for jumping between windows.
Mobile touch gestures are simpler: pan mode and horizontal scroll are gone, leaving fewer ways to trigger the wrong gesture.
Agents try to route around human-verification walls on their own before asking you to step in.
Decision questions now share one structured shape, and the unused shadow mode has been removed from the decision framework.
fixes: Long streaming responses no longer time out while tokens are still arriving.
Agents continue a batched plan when a single action in it is rejected, instead of abandoning the rest.
Settings now shows model ids you asked for even when the provider does not currently offer them.
The object creator no longer treats repeated failures as new ones because of per-run identifiers in the failure signature.
Closing a window no longer sends scene updates for its origin anchor and focus decoration mid-teardown.
The window manager logs only genuinely unknown mousedown targets, cutting log noise.

title: System One: typed decisions for agent judgment calls
summary: Agents now make their key judgment calls (finding an object, reviewing a report, deciding who takes a task) by asking a model typed questions and getting answers with probabilities, rather than working it out in free text. Each decision point can be turned off, set to advise, or set to act, and every one falls back to the old behavior when there's no decision provider.
highlights: New System One decision framework: the LLM object has a decide method that asks typed questions (choice, yes/no, score) about a state and returns every answer with its probability distribution, so callers can set their own thresholds
TypeSafe added as a decision provider (set TYPESAFE_API_KEY), with OpenRouter's System One models also available; without a decision provider, decisions run on your regular chat model

Decision points built into the system objects: Registry search ranking, Chat's report audit, ScrumMaster's quick dispatch and round review, and the plan and review steps in the creators and agents; each one can be set to off, advise, or act in Global Settings
LLM Monitor shows decision calls as their own 'Decisions' tier, whichever model handled them
Chat can now flag reports whose claims aren't grounded in what actually happened
Failed agent actions now pass along the real command or HTTP output (exit code, truncation, and a read_chunk handle for long output), so the next step can see what went wrong without re-running it
Failed tasks now stay failed, and a retry is a new corrective task scheduled by the next scrum round; tasks default to one attempt, and Chat and Goal Browser show it that way
Agents can opt out of planning polls (joinsPlanning), so internal agents like TaskReviewer no longer make an LLM call per poll just to pass
Agents that skip their first observation can set their starting think tier, so Chat's first step uses its intended lighter tier
New eye sigil favicon, now shared by the website, thin client, and desktop app
fixes: Review tasks can no longer be accepted without a verdict on whether the user-facing summary matches the latest verification
Stall warnings now fire once per stall: a goal that recovers and stalls again gets a new warning, and finished goals are cleared out

ExternalCreator judges task completion more accurately: better parse-error detection for Rust and TypeScript, read-only commands no longer mark a snapshot as tainted, and failures in files the task never touched are labeled foreign
Semantic review findings from an earlier draft no longer block tier promotion after the draft has changed
Requests that reach ObjectCreator through the job queue now keep the kind the dispatcher chose, where before every one was treated as a create-or-modify guess
abject.world no longer serves stale favicons and social cards from the CDN; content-hashed assets stay cached permanently and other static files revalidate every hour

title: A Desktop with Depth
summary: The desktop is now drawn as a real 3D scene in a new Agitprop print style, and windows move with weight when they open, close, or change. System browsers can show what they hold as live 3D maps, and your own Abjects can use the same scene, motion, and widget tools.
highlights: A 3D scene layer for the desktop: glTF models, 3D text and labels, lines and trails, sky, GPU particles, orbit cameras, and post effects, with named presets that give windows their own look
Map views in every system browser (agents, scheduler, knowledge, objects, processes, peers, collaborators): each shows its contents as an interactive 3D graph, and clicking a node inspects it

A new default look: the desktop, windows, dock, and icons are redesigned in the Agitprop print style (hard block shadows, square corners, a Constructivist backdrop); saved theme presets are migrated automatically, once
Windows move with weight: opening, closing, minimizing, restoring, and switching workspaces play motion effects with rim light and particle bursts, and any Abject can play effects on its own windows
Pop-out windows: any widget can detach into its own window and keep working, with input routed back to the original widget
A new nodeGraph widget draws force-directed graphs in 3D; lists gain search and filtering, and progress bars can show a percentage or an indeterminate state
The Eye shows live LLM activity: each call lights up its model, connections are weighted by tokens used, and a pulse marks success or failure, all without opening a window
Desktop polish: the command palette gains built-in commands, Chat folds goal trees into the conversation, and the dock, taskbar, notifications, and switcher share one consistent style
A new scene-showcase example you can load and read: it builds a live scene with models, 3D text, labels, lines, particles, sky, and camera motion
abject.world is redesigned with new screenshots and short clips of the desktop in use
fixes: Abjects can now send messages while they are shutting down, so cleanup work reaches other objects instead of being dropped; an object stopped twice no longer runs its cleanup twice
The LLM service writes its ledger to storage when it stops, so recent entries survive a shutdown
The Scheduler clears its tick timer on stop, so no stray callbacks fire after an object has stopped
The Factory accepts spawn requests with arguments wrapped by parameter name, so spawning from the Explorer method form works
Peer Network and web exposure shut down cleanly when the gateway is already stopped or was never reached
Widgets tell the objects that depend on them when they stop, so buttons, selects, split panes, and windows clean up properly

title: Clearer routing, steadier long thoughts
summary: This release makes Chat better at handling questions about your system and keeps long-running agent work from being cut off while a model is still thinking.
highlights: Chat now answers questions about your system by starting a goal instead of handing them off as a background job, so the answers are more complete and you can follow their progress. You can still ask for a background job when you want one.
fixes: Agents taking long thinking steps no longer set off the stall timer on the task that called them. Keepalive signals from the model are now passed back to the caller, so slow but healthy work isn't mistaken for a hang.

title: Steadier Answers, Smarter Budgets, Fallback Routes
summary: This release makes agents more honest about what they actually finished and more careful about how much context they spend. It also lets you set a backup model per tier so work keeps moving when a provider stumbles.
highlights: Task results that are just a bare acknowledgement (a lone "done" with nothing behind it) are now caught; the scrum master either synthesizes a real answer from the work or escalates instead of passing the empty result to Chat.
Per-tier fallback routes: each model tier can name a backup provider and model, and the Settings panel now has generalized rows for these auxiliary models.
Context-budget estimates are anchored on the provider's measured prompt token count rather than a local guess, so agents trim history based on what the model actually saw.
fixes: Gemini and OpenAI input token counts are now reported net of cached prompt tokens, so usage and budget numbers no longer double-count cache hits.

title: A steadier bridge between phone and desktop
summary: This small release is about the connection between your phone and your desktop. The link no longer keeps tearing itself down and rebuilding, and the phone view no longer refreshes over and over, so mobile sessions stay calm and responsive.
highlights: Phone-to-desktop sessions now hold a single stable WebRTC connection; before, it was replaced every few seconds
When you pick a surface in the mobile carousel, the desktop backend now switches focus to the same surface, so both sides agree on what you're looking at
fixes: Fixed a reconnect storm where the phone and desktop kept renegotiating their WebRTC link, which made the phone refresh about once a second
Fixed the mobile view reloading the surface you were already on when you picked it again in the carousel
Fixed the backend's focus drifting out of sync with the surface shown in the mobile carousel

title: Palette in Your Pocket
summary: This release brings the command palette to phones and tablets, so touch users can launch and switch windows without a keyboard. Chat windows now show a steady indicator on their icon while a goal is running, so you can see which conversations are still working.
highlights: Mobile command palette: a touch launcher opens the same command palette that Cmd+K opens on desktop, and it stays visible when the soft keyboard appears
Mobile view follows your focus: newly created, focused, or palette-launched windows now land on the view you are looking at instead of opening off-screen

Per-chat goal activity indicator: a chat window's icon shows a static marker while one of its goals is running (this replaces the earlier animated busy pulse, which cost a full window re-render every frame)
fixes: Task review no longer runs legacy recovery on its very first drain after startup, avoiding spurious recovery work at boot

title: Steadier hands, clearer signals
summary: This release makes agents more resilient when work gets long or messy: conversations that overflow the model's context recover on their own, skills can run the commands they declare, and short replies to clarification questions are understood in context. Bloom is now something you can tune per window.
highlights: Bloom is now a per-window effect: each window can carry its own glow instead of one global setting for the whole desktop
Agents recover from LLM context overflow automatically by compressing the conversation and retrying, rather than failing the task
Skills can declare the commands they need, and those commands are granted through the permission layer; command analysis in the shell now covers more cases and grants are scoped more precisely
Agent jobs gain an ask() call in their context, along with improved guidance on how agents should approach their work
fixes: Browser profile is now carried through scrum tasks, and profile parsing tolerates malformed input instead of breaking
Clarification questions are carried with the conversation, so short user replies (like "yes" or "the second one") are interpreted correctly

title: Watching the Heap
summary: This release adds a heap monitor so you can see how much memory the backend and its workers are using, and catch runaway growth before it turns into a crash.
highlights: New HeapMonitor object tracks memory usage across the worker pool and the main thread, sampling heap size over time so leaks show up as a trend instead of a surprise.
Process Explorer gains a heap strip: a compact per-process view of memory use that sits alongside the existing process list.

title: Steadier Memory for Long-Running Sessions
summary: This is a small maintenance release focused on stability. It fixes memory leaks in the worker pool so Abject can run for long stretches without slowly using more and more memory.
highlights: Long-running sessions stay stable: the background workers that host your objects no longer accumulate memory over time, which could eventually crash a worker after many hours of use
fixes: Plugged several memory leaks in the worker pool plumbing (bookkeeping for in-flight messages and spawned objects is now cleaned up properly)

title: Steadier Phones, Tidier Timers
summary: This release makes the phone client show abject content correctly and removes a source of memory growth and storage load on long-running desktops. It also fixes a peer connection error during reconnects.
highlights: Phone client: abjects that draw through the 3D scene now render correctly in the focused view and on the active card in the card overview.
Timers are now managed by the Abject base class: agent and UI timers are cancelled automatically when an object stops, so stopped objects no longer leave timers running in long sessions.
Shared state skips rewriting its manifest when you re-set a key that is already persisted, which cuts storage work during busy periods.
Tainted-canvas diagnostics (canvases blocked by cross-origin images) are now relayed from the client, which makes rendering problems on remote and mobile clients easier to trace.
fixes: Peer connections drop stale SDP answers that arrive after a negotiation reset, so they no longer cause connection errors during reconnects.
The task reviewer now guards against invalid run timestamps instead of failing on them.
Scene-rendered abject content no longer renders incorrectly on the phone client.

title: Typing that lands, traffic that remembers
summary: Mobile typing on Android Chrome now arrives reliably, and every object's HTTP traffic is recorded as redacted cassettes you can replay and inspect.
highlights: HTTP cassettes: each user-created object's HTTP exchanges are recorded by a new CassetteRecorder, keyed by the object's typeId and spawned permanently at boot (worker-eligible).
Exchanges are redacted before they leave the HTTP client, sent straight to the recorder, and skip the LLM at the source; redaction is linear and form-scoped so large bodies stay cheap.
Mobile typing on Android Chrome no longer drops characters: IME and autocorrect text is delivered through proxy value deltas, and the keyboard proxy keeps focus during surface churn.
The dock and toasts never steal keyboard focus (new focusOnCreate option for windows).
The default Peer Network window is wider so all six tabs fit.
fixes: Keydown events delivered to a scene node now fall through to surface routing instead of being swallowed.
Cassette flush deferral is bounded by a max-wait window so recordings cannot be postponed indefinitely.
Redaction of HTTP exchange bodies is linear-time and limited to form fields, fixing slow or over-broad scrubbing.

title: Your desktop, reachable from a browser
summary: This release lets you serve a workspace over plain HTTP, so anything you build in Abject can be opened from a regular browser on your network. It also keeps a workspace running when a worker thread dies, and stops long agent sessions from growing without bound.
highlights: New Web Gateway object serves plain HTTP on a port you choose, so workspaces can be reached from an ordinary browser instead of only through the Abject client
New Web Access tab in the Network UI, with per-workspace settings for what is exposed to the web
The runtime now rebuilds objects after a pool worker dies, so a crashed worker no longer leaves a workspace with missing objects
fixes: The server answers plain HTTP requests properly instead of returning 426 Upgrade Required, so browsers and tools like curl get a real response
Task sessions and review reports no longer grow without bound during long agent runs

title: Guarded Projects, Gentler Forgetting
summary: Abject 0.10.1 makes the system more careful with what it touches: external projects stay inside their own root, forgetting knowledge takes two deliberate steps, and objects notice when their registrations go stale. Settings now persist globally and the site gets accurate install and why pages.
highlights: External projects are guarded against writes outside their project root, so agents working on a registered codebase cannot stray into the rest of your disk.
Forgetting knowledge is now a two-step act: the first forget archives the entry, and a second forget deletes it for good.
Objects detect stale registrations through manifest freshness checks and re-sync themselves with the Registry automatically.
Heartbeats and taskId scoping tighten how long-running work is tracked across objects.
Global settings now persist across sessions instead of resetting each launch.
The abject.world site received an accuracy pass, new install and why pages, and OS-aware download links.
Mac build targets updated for the desktop app.
fixes: Agent descriptions are kept in full in the ScrumMaster team roster instead of being truncated, so task routing sees each agent's real abilities.

title: Agents that remember, learn, and know their limits
summary: Agents now carry context across goals, reuse what they already agreed on, and learn from evidence instead of assumptions. Shared workspaces gain collaboration UI and collaborative goals, and every kind of session (local, peer, and CLI provider) gets firmer boundaries.
highlights: Agents keep conversation context across goals, reuse accepted proposals when a goal continues, and run under explicit step budgets with permission-aware asks
Task outcomes now feed a world model: agents reconcile knowledge with verification evidence, record runtime action evidence, and revise patterns with automatic provenance and review settlement
Shared workspaces get a collaboration UI, collaborative goal tracking, per-entry knowledge synchronization, and workspace-scoped state routed to native peers
Peer identity is bound to authenticated session epochs, and each object declares how far a copy of it may travel
Durable agent sessions with trustworthy outcomes and adaptive scrum rounds; verification and cancellation now settle reliably
New PeerLLM provider lets one peer serve models to another, with planning controls; native CLI providers run inside enforced execution boundaries and have their models discovered rather than pinned
Object creators bind acceptance to the live object and its project revision, so a proposal is judged against what actually exists
Task-scoped processes and conditional file writes give capabilities safer, cleaner cleanup
Box layouts report and surface overflow, and Settings supports dynamic widget layouts
Chat browser can search inside conversation content, not just titles
fixes: Planners are preserved during scrum dispatch instead of being dropped mid-goal
Review settlement and output paging corrected for long agent runs
Action parsing hardened and loop guidance improved for agent harness reliability and concurrency
A signaling drop during ICE candidate exchange can no longer kill the process (fence narrowed to the one call and its exception)
LLM requests use the model's sampling defaults and account usage to the sender; retries accept a per-error delay override
Antigravity CLI provider gets explicit tier defaults and instantly resamples empty completions

title: Clean Exits, Steady Handoffs
summary: A small stability release. The Linux desktop app now quits cleanly, and web agents keep reporting progress while you take the wheel.
highlights: Stability fixes for desktop shutdown and for web agent tasks during human handoffs.
fixes: The Linux AppImage no longer hangs on shutdown; quitting the app exits cleanly.
Web agent tasks no longer appear stalled when a human takes over the browser; the progress heartbeat stays alive through the handoff.

title: Smarter permissions, sturdier workspaces
summary: This release rethinks how Abject decides what a command may do, and fixes a serious bug where deleting one workspace could destroy the system objects every workspace depends on.
highlights: Permission decisions are now based on what a command actually does and where it runs, so approvals reflect real behavior rather than the command's name
Approving a permission request now covers the exact command that asked for it; you will no longer be re-prompted for the thing you just allowed
fixes: Deleting a workspace no longer destroys the global system objects shared by all workspaces
A question dialog on screen now holds its calling objects open until you answer, so replies no longer arrive at objects that have already shut down
The desktop app enforces one instance per data directory and no longer attempts to show dialogs after its pipe has closed

title: Patterns Take Shape
summary: The knowledge base now stores learned patterns as real structure instead of free-form prose, so agents can link, reuse, and repair them reliably. A small release with one meaningful upgrade to how your objects remember what works.
highlights: Learned patterns are now saved as structured knowledge with explicit links between related entries, instead of blocks of prose; agents can follow those links to find and apply related patterns
Existing patterns that were stored as prose are automatically healed into the new structured form, so nothing you have already taught the system is lost
fixes: Peer-to-peer networking no longer starts building new peer connections while the app is shutting down, which could leave stray connections behind

title: Stop Means Stop
summary: A small patch release focused on one thing: when you cancel a goal, your agents now actually stop. No new features, just a more obedient system.
highlights: Canceling a goal now takes effect promptly: agents check for cancellation between task steps instead of finishing every remaining step first.
fixes: Agents no longer keep working through queued task steps after their goal has been cancelled; cancellation is honored at each step boundary.

title: Nothing Left Behind
summary: This release is about leaving cleanly. Quitting Abject now takes every helper process with it on every platform, so nothing keeps running (or crashing) after you close the app.
highlights: Quitting is now thorough: the app exits through Electron and shuts down all of its child processes with it, instead of leaving helpers behind.
MCP servers are stopped completely: Abject terminates the server's whole process tree, not just the shell that launched it, so no tool processes linger after shutdown.
Process cleanup now works the same on Windows, which lacks process groups: Abject walks the process tree there too, so Windows users get the same clean exit.
fixes: Fixed a crash on exit: the peer-to-peer networking layer (libdatachannel) is now shut down in an orderly way instead of aborting as the app closes.
Fixed orphaned MCP server processes that survived because only the wrapper shell in front of them was killed.
Fixed leftover child processes on Windows after quitting the app.

title: Parallel agents, plans as graphs
summary: Agents can now take on several tasks at once, and planners lay out each round of work as a dependency graph so multi-step goals run in the right order. A new ExternalCreator agent brings that work out of the workspace and onto your disk, authoring real projects as ordinary files.
highlights: New ExternalCreator agent: an authoring agent that creates and maintains projects on disk, working with real files instead of only objects inside a workspace.
Agents can run several tasks at the same time, and edits that target the same file are serialized so parallel work never clobbers itself.
Planners now express a scrum round as a dependency graph rather than a flat list, so steps that depend on each other are easy to state and run in the right order.

Smarter goal handling: the system first asks whether a goal breaks into sub-tasks before asking who should own it, and planners no longer add a final task whose only job is to assemble what the parts already wrote down.
Jobs can name an object as a recipient, so work can be routed to an object by its name without knowing its internal id.
Every LLM call is attributed to the agent that made it, and streamed output is routed by request correlation, so live output and usage stay accurate while agents work in parallel.
The CLI gateway now derives its port from WS_PORT, so custom backend ports work with the commune CLI without extra configuration.
fixes: Cancelling a task now frees its queue slot; previously a slot could stay occupied with nothing running in it, quietly shrinking an agent's capacity.
A batch of work that ends in a terminal action (such as asking the user a question) now closes properly instead of hanging open.
Fixed the agy provider's stream-json input discriminator, which broke parsing of streamed input.

title: Antigravity Lands
summary: Abject can now use the Antigravity CLI (agy) as an LLM provider, joining the other CLI providers your objects can think through. A round of follow-up fixes makes it dependable from day one: a correct model catalog, resilient streaming, and runs that report progress and shut down cleanly.
highlights: New LLM provider: the Antigravity CLI (agy). If you have agy installed, your objects can use it for their thinking, right alongside the existing CLI providers.
The agy provider ships hardened, not just added: it inherits everything the other CLI providers already learned, with a corrected model catalog and a sturdier streaming path.
fixes: Long-running agy goals no longer stall silently: progress keepalives fire every 5 seconds, and a SIGKILL fallback cleans up processes that refuse to exit.
SkillAgent now advertises the host's ShellExecutor CLI capability in its ask prompt, so work that needs a shell gets routed to an agent that actually has one.

title: CLI Providers, Warm and Separate
summary: The CLI-based LLM providers now run as persistent terminal sessions instead of spawning a fresh process for every request, so responses start faster. Each CLI transport is also listed as its own provider, so you choose the one you want rather than having the system pick for you.
highlights: Both CLI transports are offered as separate providers: pick the one you want in settings instead of getting an automatic choice
CLI providers run as warm terminal sessions kept alive between requests, replacing the one-process-per-request model (less startup overhead on each call)

title: Every LLM Call, Accounted For
summary: Abject now keeps a ledger of every LLM call it makes, including what each one cost. The Eye shows the running record, so you can see where your tokens and money actually go.
highlights: An LLM call ledger records each request your objects make, with per-call cost
The Eye displays the ledger, giving you a live view of spending across the system

title: Bulk Results Off The Critical Path
